newsitem.title: POLAND: RAIN THREATENS MORE FLOODS IN CENTRAL EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: RAIN THREATENS MORE FLOODS IN CENTRAL EUROPE.

text.p: Rain lashed Poland and the Czech Republic anew on Friday, threatening a ruinous new wave in flooding that has already killed 93 people and wrecked many thousands of homes and businesses.
The skies also opened up over neighbouring Austria, putting wide areas of that country on flood alert as swollen rivers came close to spilling over their banks.
"It is raining, from Koszalin (in the north) through all of western Poland, with varying intensity," Polish flood crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said.
"The situation doesn't look good," he told Reuters.

The new precipitation tormenting Poles and Czechs was not as intense as at the outset of the two-week-old flood crisis. But the ground was now so soggy and rivers so high that they could scarcely absorb any more water, officials said.

"The rains are dangerous even though we estimate they will be only one third of the great downpours which hit us over a dozen days ago," said Krzysztof Szamalek, a deputy environment minister on Poland's crisis committee, told public radio.
Parliament, sitting deep into the night, passed more than 20 bills allowing the government to increase borrowing and rush both funds and rescue assistance to stricken areas.

High finance was far from the minds of exhausted Poles who faced a repeat of the nightmare that swamped more than 4,000 sq km of land and 970 towns and villages, leaving a shroud of filth and the risk of epidemic in its wake.
Flags were at half mast, churches held services and public broadcasters played solemn music to mark a day of mourning for the 48 people killed so far in the inundation.

In the Czech Republic, where flood tides have left 45 dead with two people missing in the country's worst natural calamity this century, light rain began falling overnight but full-blown storms were forecast for the weekend.
Thousands of houses have been destroyed or badly damaged, road, rail and telecommunications links have been cut and valuable industrial and agricultural land has been swamped.
This has been a terrible financial blow to the emerging free-market country of 10.5 million people.
Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz telephoned Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec on Thursday to discuss efforts to fight the floods, a Czech diplomatic source said.
A Polish government spokeswoman said last week the Czechs had emptied reservoirs on the Odra river, which runs though Poland, and that this had worsened the situation there.

But Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati, visiting Prague, said no official criticism was implied. He said the two countries, which share a number of rivers, had been coordinating flood efforts well.
In Austria, meteorologist Manfred Bauer predicted a flood catastrophe if downpours kept up in the regions of Lower Austria, Styria, Salzburg and Upper Austria. REUTER
